entries.title: No Other Gospel: The Finality of the Apostolic Message
entries.content_summary: Stott shows that Paul opens not with his customary thanksgiving but with astonishment and alarm, because the Galatians are deserting the God who called them and turning to a different gospel. Stott stresses that Paul's point is that there is really no other gospel at all; the rival message of the Judaizers, which adds circumcision and law-keeping to faith in Christ, is not an alternative version of the good news but a perversion that destroys it. So grave is the matter that Paul pronounces a solemn curse on anyone, even himself or an angel from heaven, who should preach a gospel other than the one they received. Stott presses the seriousness: the gospel is not human opinion open to revision but the fixed, God-given truth of salvation by grace, and to tamper with it is to imperil souls.
entries.content_detail:
Stott draws attention to the abruptness of the letter's opening. Every other Pauline letter begins with thanksgiving, but here Paul is too disturbed to give thanks. He is astonished, and the tense suggests the defection is happening even as he writes: the Galatians are in the act of turning away. Stott is careful about the object of their desertion; Paul says they are deserting not merely a doctrine but the God who called them by the grace of Christ. To abandon the gospel of grace is to abandon the God of grace.

The heart of the passage is Paul's insistence that the message troubling the churches is not a legitimate variant of the gospel. Stott explains the situation: false teachers, commonly called Judaizers, were insisting that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be true Christians, adding law-works to faith as a condition of acceptance with God. Paul will not allow this to be described as another gospel, because there is no other. Any message that adds human works to the finished work of Christ is not a different good news but a contradiction of the only good news, and Stott underlines that such an addition does not enrich the gospel but overthrows it.

Stott gives full weight to the double curse of 1:8-9. Paul says that if he himself, or even an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel contrary to the one the Galatians received, let him be accursed, and he repeats it for emphasis. Stott reads this not as intemperate anger but as a measure of what is at stake. Because the gospel is the way of salvation, to corrupt it is to endanger the eternal welfare of those who believe it; a false gospel cannot save. Moreover, Stott notes, Paul subordinates even apostolic and angelic authority to the gospel itself: the message is not validated by the messenger, but the messenger is judged by the message. The gospel is God's, received by revelation and not of human origin, and therefore it is fixed and final. No church, no apostle, no angel has the authority to change it. For Stott this establishes the theme of the whole letter: the defence of the one true gospel of justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

entries.title: Justified by Faith in Christ, Not by Works of the Law
entries.content_summary: Stott reaches the doctrinal heart of the letter in Paul's statement that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Stott defines justification as a legal term: it is God's act of declaring a sinner righteous, of accepting and acquitting the guilty, not of making them morally good. The great question the verse settles is on what basis God accepts us, and Paul's answer is emphatic and exclusive. It is not by works of the law, not by anything we do, but through faith in Christ. Stott notes that Paul says this even of himself and Peter, Jews by birth who knew the law, yet who believed in Christ precisely in order to be justified by faith and not by works, since by works of the law no one will be justified.
entries.content_detail:
Stott sees these verses, arising from Paul's confrontation with Peter at Antioch, as the doctrinal centre of Galatians, the clearest single statement of the truth the whole letter defends. Peter, under pressure from certain men, had withdrawn from table fellowship with Gentile believers, and Paul saw that his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel. The principle Paul draws out in response is justification by faith alone.

Stott is careful to define his terms, because the word justify is easily misunderstood. He insists that it is a legal or forensic term, drawn from the law court, and that its opposite is condemnation. To justify is not to make a person righteous in character but to declare a person righteous in status, to accept and acquit them before God. The doctrine of justification therefore answers the most fundamental of all questions: how can guilty sinners be accepted by a holy God?

Paul's answer, Stott stresses, is framed both negatively and positively, and the two must be held together. Negatively, no one is justified by works of the law. Stott takes this to mean not merely the ceremonial law but law-keeping as such; nothing we do can be the ground of our acceptance, because our best works are stained and our record is one of failure. Positively, justification is through faith in Jesus Christ. Faith, Stott repeats throughout the letter, is not itself a work or a merit but the receiving of what Christ has done; it is the empty hand that takes God's gift.

Stott underlines the force of Paul's argument that even he and Peter, Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners, had come to believe in Christ for this very reason, that they might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. If lifelong keepers of the law needed to be justified by faith, how much more everyone else. And Paul clinches it by echoing the psalmist: by works of the law no human being will be justified. Stott presses the exclusiveness of the word faith here; the moment works are added as a ground of acceptance, grace is nullified and Christ died for nothing. The whole gospel stands or falls on this single point, that we are justified by faith in Christ and not by our own works.

entries.title: Crucified with Christ: Christ Lives in Me
entries.chapter_or_episode: Galatians 2:20 (The believer's union with the crucified Christ)
entries.content_summary: Stott expounds this famous verse as Paul's testimony to the personal reality of union with Christ. To be justified by faith is to be joined to Christ, and Paul describes that union in the language of death and new life: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Stott is careful to say that the self is not annihilated; Paul goes on to speak of the life he now lives in the body. Rather, the old self, the person under law and condemnation, has died with Christ, and a new life has begun, indwelt and animated by Christ himself. This new life is lived by faith in the Son of God, and Stott dwells on the personal note of its ground: Christ loved me and gave himself for me.
entries.content_detail:
Stott regards Galatians 2:20 as one of the most personal and profound verses Paul ever wrote, and he treats it as the experiential counterpart to the doctrine just stated. Justification by faith is not a cold transaction; it brings the believer into living union with Christ. Paul expresses that union first in terms of death: I have been crucified with Christ. Stott connects this with the broader New Testament teaching that in Christ's death the believer died, so that the old life under law and under sin's condemnation was brought to an end. The believer is not merely a spectator of the cross but a participant in it.

Stott then handles the striking paradox of the verse, that it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. He is anxious to guard against a mystical misreading in which the human personality is dissolved. Paul does not mean that he has ceased to be himself, for he immediately speaks of the life he now lives in the flesh, in the body, as a continuing personal existence. What has died is the old self, the person Paul was under the law, trying to establish his own righteousness; what now lives is a self renewed and possessed by Christ. Stott summarizes it as a change of centre and of master: the ego has been dethroned and Christ enthroned, so that Christ's indwelling life becomes the animating principle of the believer's own.

Stott lays weight on the means by which this new life is sustained. Paul says the life he now lives he lives by faith in the Son of God. Faith is therefore not only the way we are first justified but the daily principle of the new life; the Christian lives, moment by moment, by trusting and drawing upon Christ. And Stott lingers over the deeply personal ground Paul gives for this faith, that the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. He observes how Paul makes the universal truth of the atonement intensely individual, appropriating for himself what Christ did for all. The love that gave itself on the cross is not merely love for the world in general but love for me in particular. For Stott this is the secret of Christian living: a life lived out of union with a Christ who died in our place and now lives within us, received and sustained by a faith that rests on his personal love.

entries.title: Christ Became a Curse for Us: The Blessing of Abraham
entries.chapter_or_episode: Galatians 3:10-14 (Redeemed from the curse of the law)
entries.content_summary: Stott expounds Paul's argument that all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, since the law pronounces its curse on everyone who fails to keep it perfectly, and no one does. The good news is that Christ redeemed us from that curse by becoming a curse for us, for it is written that anyone hung on a tree is cursed. Stott reads this as plain substitution: on the cross Christ bore the curse we had earned, standing in our place under the judgment of God. The purpose was that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ, and that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Stott stresses that the curse and the blessing are exchanged at the cross: Christ takes our curse so that we may receive Abraham's blessing.
entries.content_detail:
Stott follows Paul's tightly argued case that the law can only condemn those who look to it for justification. The reasoning begins with a stark alternative: those who rely on works of the law are under a curse, because Scripture itself pronounces a curse on everyone who does not continue in all things written in the law to do them. Stott presses the word all: the law demands not partial but perfect and perpetual obedience, and since no one renders it, the law can bring the law-reliant only condemnation. Paul reinforces this with Habakkuk's principle that the righteous shall live by faith, showing that law and faith operate on opposite principles; the law says do and live, but faith receives what God gives.

Against this dark background Stott sets the gospel of 3:13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. Stott takes redeemed in its full sense of purchasing release at a price, and he reads the verse as one of the clearest statements of substitutionary atonement in Paul. The curse that the law pronounced on us, our due penalty for breaking it, Christ took upon himself. Paul grounds this in the words of Deuteronomy that everyone hung on a tree is under God's curse; Stott explains that the manner of Jesus' death, crucifixion, publicly marked him out as bearing a curse, and that this curse was not his own but ours. He stood in our place, under the judgment we deserved, so that we might go free.

Stott then draws out the double purpose Paul states in 3:14. The first is that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. The blessing God had promised to Abraham, that in him all nations would be blessed, is nothing less than justification and acceptance with God, and it now flows out to the nations, not through law or circumcision, but through Christ. The second purpose is that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Stott notes how the two verses effect a great exchange: Christ takes our curse, and we receive Abraham's blessing and the gift of the Spirit. He stresses that all of this comes through faith and not through works, so that the argument returns to the letter's central theme. The cross is the place where curse and blessing change hands.

entries.title: The Law as Guardian Until Christ Came
entries.chapter_or_episode: Galatians 3:19-25 (The purpose and end of the law)
entries.content_summary: Stott addresses the question Paul's argument provokes: if we are justified by faith and not by law, why was the law given at all? Paul answers that the law was added because of transgressions, to expose and even to increase the awareness of sin, and that it was temporary, in force until the promised offspring, Christ, should come. Stott expounds the image of the law as a paidagogos, the household guardian or custodian who supervised a child until the age of maturity. The law was not the way of salvation but a temporary custodian that shut us up under sin and led us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. Now that faith has come, Stott stresses, we are no longer under this guardian; the law's supervisory role has ended, and in Christ we have reached our maturity as sons.
entries.content_detail:
Stott recognizes that Paul's exaltation of the promise over the law raises an obvious objection: if the law cannot justify and came four hundred and thirty years after the promise to Abraham, does it have any purpose, and does it perhaps conflict with the promise? Paul's answer is a firm no; the law and the promise do not compete but play different roles in God's single plan. The law was not given to justify but for other ends, and Stott sets out the two Paul emphasizes.

First, the law was added because of transgressions. Stott explains that the law's function was to reveal sin, to define it, and even to provoke and multiply it, turning wrongdoing into conscious transgression against a known command. Far from making people righteous, the law exposed their unrighteousness and made their guilt plain, so that Scripture consigned everything under sin. Second, the law was temporary, given until the offspring should come to whom the promise referred, that is, Christ. It was an interim measure with a built-in expiry, always pointing beyond itself to the fulfilment in Christ.

The heart of Stott's exposition is Paul's image in 3:24 of the law as a paidagogos, which he is careful to explain, since the modern word schoolmaster or tutor can mislead. In the Greco-Roman household the paidagogos was not the teacher but a trusted slave who had charge of a boy in his minority, escorting him to school, supervising his conduct, and exercising a strict, temporary discipline until the child came of age. Stott applies this to the law's role in the history of salvation and in personal experience alike: the law was our custodian, keeping us under restraint and under condemnation, but its very severity drove us to seek the freedom that is in Christ. So the law was our guardian until Christ, that we might be justified by faith.

Stott then presses Paul's decisive conclusion in 3:25: now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. With the coming of Christ the custodial role of the law has ended, not because the law was bad but because its purpose has been served and the age of maturity has arrived. Stott is careful to say this does not abolish the moral law as a standard, but it does end the law as a way of acceptance and as a regime of tutelage. In Christ, believers have grown up into the full status of sons, and this leads directly into the next great theme of adoption and freedom.

entries.title: From Slaves to Sons: Adoption, the Spirit, and Freedom
entries.content_summary: Stott expounds the transition Paul describes from slavery under the law to the freedom of sons. In the fullness of time God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. Stott stresses the deliberate double sending: God sent his Son to secure our status as sons, and then sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father,' to assure us of it. So we are no longer slaves but sons, and if sons, then heirs. On this basis Paul issues the great charge of 5:1: it was for freedom that Christ set us free, so stand firm and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery. Stott sees Christian liberty as the birthright of the adopted, to be guarded against every attempt to re-impose the law.
entries.content_detail:
Stott reads Galatians 4 as the climax of Paul's argument about the law, moving from the legal category of justification to the family category of adoption. Paul illustrates the change with the picture of an heir who, while still a child, is no different in practice from a slave, being under guardians and trustees until the time set by his father. So it was with God's people under the law; they were in a state of minority and bondage. But the situation has been transformed by a decisive divine act.

Stott gives careful attention to the great statement of 4:4-5, that when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. He notes the marks of the incarnation compressed here: the Son's pre-existence implied in his being sent, his true humanity in being born of a woman, and his placement under the law that he might redeem those enslaved by it. The purpose of this redemption is adoption, the granting of full filial status to those who were slaves. Stott stresses that adoption is not the same as regeneration; it is the legal bestowal of the standing and privileges of sons upon those brought into God's family.

Stott then highlights the second sending in 4:6. Because we are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. He observes the trinitarian shape of salvation here: the Father sends the Son to give us the status of sons, and then sends the Spirit of the Son to assure us of it. The cry Abba is the Spirit's witness within, so that sonship is not only a legal fact but a felt reality. The conclusion Paul draws is triumphant: so you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.

Stott then carries this straight into 5:1, the hinge between the doctrinal and practical halves of the letter. For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery. Stott presents Christian freedom as the birthright of the adopted son, freedom from the law as a way of acceptance, from its curse and its bondage. And he stresses the urgency of Paul's command to stand firm: this liberty is precious and precarious, constantly threatened by the false teachers who would re-impose circumcision and law-keeping. To return to the law after being freed by Christ is to exchange sonship for slavery all over again, and Paul will not allow it.

entries.title: The Spirit Against the Flesh, and the Fruit of the Spirit
entries.content_summary: Stott shows how Paul guards Christian freedom from being misused as license. Freedom is not an excuse for the flesh but the opportunity to serve one another in love and to walk by the Spirit. The believer is caught in a real conflict, for the flesh desires what is against the Spirit and the Spirit what is against the flesh, and the two are opposed. Stott sets Paul's two lists side by side: the works of the flesh, the ugly and self-centred products of fallen nature, and the fruit of the Spirit, the beautiful cluster of Christ-like graces beginning with love. Stott stresses that this fruit is not self-generated but grown by the Spirit in those who walk by him, and he underlines Paul's summons to keep in step with the Spirit, since those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
entries.content_detail:
Stott presents this section as Paul's answer to a natural fear: if Christians are free from the law, what is to restrain them from sin? Paul's reply is that Christian liberty is not lawlessness but life in the Spirit. Freedom is not to be used as an opportunity for the flesh; rather, through love believers are to serve one another, and indeed the whole law is fulfilled in the command to love your neighbour as yourself. Stott notes the irony that the very love the law required is produced not by the law but by the Spirit in those set free from it.

The governing command of the passage, Stott observes, is to walk by the Spirit, with the promise that those who do so will not gratify the desires of the flesh. He then expounds the reality of the Christian's inner conflict in 5:17: the flesh, our fallen self-centred nature, and the Spirit are locked in opposition, each desiring what is contrary to the other, so that the believer cannot simply do as he pleases. Stott is realistic about this warfare: the Christian life is a genuine and lifelong struggle. Yet the outcome is not in doubt for those who walk by the Spirit, and Stott points out that being led by the Spirit is itself evidence of being free from the law's condemnation.

Stott then works through the two contrasting lists Paul draws up. The works of the flesh are many and varied, ranging over sexual sin, false religion, social discord, and excess; Stott notes that they are called works, the busy output of unaided human nature, and that they are largely destructive of community as well as of the self. Over against them stands the fruit of the Spirit, and Stott dwells on the deliberate change of number: not works but fruit, singular, a single ripening cluster grown by the Spirit rather than manufactured by effort. He notes that the list begins with love and unfolds into joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control, and that these graces together form a portrait of the character of Christ himself, reproduced in the believer by the Spirit.

Stott closes with Paul's summary in 5:24-25. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires; the decisive break has been made. Therefore, since we live by the Spirit, we are also to keep in step with the Spirit, walking in line with him day by day. For Stott the message is that holiness is neither law-keeping nor self-effort but the fruit of a Spirit-directed life, in which freedom expresses itself not in self-indulgence but in the character and love of Christ.

entries.title: Boasting Only in the Cross, and the New Creation
entries.content_summary: Stott shows how Paul, taking up the pen himself, sums up the whole letter by contrasting two kinds of religion. The false teachers want to boast in the flesh, compelling circumcision to make a good outward showing and to avoid persecution for the cross. Paul, by contrast, will boast in nothing except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. Stott stresses that the cross is the ground of the Christian's whole confidence and the death of all self-glory. What matters, Paul concludes, is neither circumcision nor uncircumcision but a new creation. Stott reads this as the letter's final verdict: external religious marks count for nothing, and everything depends on the inward transformation God works, so that the believer is a new creation in Christ.
entries.content_detail:
Stott notes that Paul takes the pen from his secretary to write the closing paragraph in his own large letters, a sign of the personal urgency with which he presses home the letter's message. In these final verses Paul sets two rival religions side by side and lays bare their motives, and Stott draws the contrast sharply because it gathers up everything the letter has argued.

On one side are the Judaizers. Stott exposes the motives Paul attributes to them: they want to make a good showing in the flesh, to point to the outward mark of circumcision as evidence of religious success, and they press it on the Galatians in order to avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ. Their religion is external, self-advertising, and cowardly, concerned with human approval and human boasting. Stott observes Paul's cutting point that they do not even keep the law themselves; their interest is not obedience but the credit of having circumcised converts to boast about.

Over against this Paul sets his own confession in 6:14, which Stott treats as one of the noblest statements in the letter: far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Stott stresses the totality of it. The cross, an instrument of shame and the symbol of everything the world despised, has become the Christian's only ground of boasting, because there alone is salvation found. And the cross has effected a mutual crucifixion: through it the world has been crucified to Paul, and Paul to the world. Stott explains that the values, approval, and standards of the world are now dead to the man who glories in the cross, and he is dead to them; the cross has severed the old allegiance and cut the nerve of self-glory.

Stott then draws out Paul's final verdict in 6:15, which he sees as the summary of the whole epistle: neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. External religious marks, the very things over which the whole controversy raged, are declared to be of no account. What matters is that God makes a person new, a new creation in Christ. Stott underlines that this is the ultimate issue: not ritual, not law-keeping, not the flesh, but the inward, transforming work of God. Upon all who walk by this rule Paul pronounces peace and mercy, and calls them the Israel of God, the true people of God defined not by circumcision but by faith and new birth. So the letter that began by defending the one true gospel ends by locating everything in the cross and the new creation it brings.
